title: Data Dictionary
text:
This page documents the data behind Island Time, Interrupted: where the information came from, what each indicator measures, how the datasets are structured, and what limitations affect their use.
The Methodology explains how these data were selected, combined, and analyzed. The Technical Analysis presents the findings.

title: Data Dictionary
text:
Tourism Indicators

International visitor spending (% of GDP)
Primary indicator



Field
Description




Source
UN Tourism statistics, national statistical organizations and central banks, OECD national accounts, and World Bank staff estimates, processed by Our World in Data


Publisher
Our World in Data


Analytical variable
visitor_spend_gdp_pct


Baseline variables
vspend_mean_1519, vspend_mean_1719


Unit
Percent of GDP


Available years
1995–2024


Use
Primary explanatory indicator for shock analysis



What it measures
Spending by international visitors in the destination economy, expressed relative to the economy’s GDP. It includes spending on accommodation, food, transport, entertainment, shopping, and fares paid to domestic airlines.
The indicator provides a measure of the scale of international visitor spending relative to the overall economy. A higher value suggests greater exposure to international visitor demand.
Use in this project
This is the primary explanatory indicator in the shock analysis. Its relatively broad coverage makes it more suitable for cross-economy comparison than the available tourism direct GDP series.



International tourism receipts (% of total exports)



Field
Description




Source
World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI)


Indicator code
ST.INT.RCPT.XP.ZS


Analytical variable
tourism_receipts_pct_exports


Baseline variables
receipts_mean_1519, receipts_mean_1719


Unit
Percent of total exports of goods and services


Available years
Approximately 1995–2020


Use
Complementary explanatory indicator for shock analysis



What it measures
International tourism receipts relative to the total value of exports of goods and services. Receipts represent payments made to a destination economy by international visitors for goods and services consumed during their trips.
Coverage limitations
Fourteen of the 35 economies in the WDI shock sample lack a 2019 observation. Their 2017–2019 baselines therefore rely on 2017 and 2018 only.
This uneven coverage is important when comparing the WDI results with those from OWID.
Use in this project
A complementary tourism exposure measure. It is used in its own shock sample and in the common-sample comparison, allowing the analysis to test whether the observed relationship depends on the choice of tourism indicator.

title: Data Dictionary
text:
Economic Indicators
Economic outcome data come primarily from the World Bank’s World Development Indicators.

GDP growth (annual %)



Field
Description




Source
World Bank, WDI


Indicator code
NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG


Analytical variable
gdp_growth_pct


Derived variable
gdp_growth_pct_2020


Unit
Annual percent change


Prices
Constant 2015 prices


Use
Outcome variable for 2020 shock regressions



What it measures
The annual percentage change in real gross domestic product. It captures the change in the volume of economic output, excluding the effects of price changes.
Use in this project
The primary outcome variable in the 2020 shock regressions. It measures the economy-wide contraction during the first pandemic year.
Limitations
Annual GDP growth aggregates activity across the entire calendar year. It does not capture the precise timing of travel restrictions, differences in the duration of economic disruption, or the distribution of economic losses among households and industries.
It also cannot distinguish pandemic-related effects from other economic developments occurring in the same year.



Real GDP (constant 2015 USD)



Field
Description




Source
World Bank, WDI


Indicator code
NY.GDP.MKTP.KD


Analytical variable
gdp_real_const2015usd


Unit
Constant 2015 US dollars


Use
Outcome variable for recovery analysis



What it measures
The total value of domestic production, expressed in constant 2015 US dollars. Constant-price values remove the effect of changes in prices over time, allowing comparisons of real output across years.
Use in this project
The primary measure of aggregate recovery. Each economy’s annual value is indexed to its 2019 level, with 2019 set equal to 100.
Coverage
Within the 29-economy shock sample:

2015–2022: 29 economies
2023–2024: 28 economies
2025: 22 economies, with preliminary estimates




Real GDP per capita (constant 2015 USD)



Field
Description




Source
World Bank, WDI


Indicator code
NY.GDP.PCAP.KD


Analytical variable
gdppc_real_const2015usd


Unit
Constant 2015 US dollars per person


Use
Per-capita economic recovery



What it measures
Real GDP divided by the population, expressed in constant 2015 US dollars per person.
Use in this project
A complementary recovery measure. It distinguishes the recovery of total economic output from the recovery of output relative to population.

Coverage and Comparability
The two principal tourism indicators have different coverage profiles. That difference affects which economies can be compared and how much confidence to place in comparisons across specifications.








Indicator
Latest year in current retrieval
Key coverage issue




OWID visitor spending (% GDP)
2024
Broadest coverage in the shock sample


WDI tourism receipts (% exports)
2020
No observations after 2020; 14 of 35 WDI shock-sample economies lack 2019


WDI real GDP
2025
2025 coverage limited to 22 economies and preliminary



The common sample of 24 economies allows the two principal tourism indicators to be compared without changing the country set.
Even within that sample, the indicators can produce different estimates because their denominators and underlying coverage differ.
Missing data should not be interpreted as zero tourism, zero economic activity, or absence of an economic relationship. It means the relevant source did not provide an observation suitable for that comparison.

title: Data Dictionary
text:
Source Notes and Limitations
Several limitations apply across the data inventory:

Different statistical concepts: Gross visitor spending and tourism receipts measure different things. Their values should not be substituted for one another.
Uneven national reporting: International tourism statistics depend on national collection and reporting systems. Definitions and coverage can vary.
Incomplete territorial coverage: Some non-sovereign territories and smaller island economies are not recognized by the World Bank API or are missing from particular OWID datasets.
Uneven time coverage: Tourism and economic indicators do not necessarily cover the same years or economies. The analysis documents these differences rather than filling gaps with assumed values.
Revisions and preliminary estimates: Source datasets can be revised. The 2025 GDP observations are preliminary in the current retrieval and should not be treated as final.
National aggregates: GDP and tourism indicators describe economy-wide activity. They do not directly measure the distribution of gains and losses among residents.

The processed datasets preserve the distinctions between source observations, constructed baselines, and indexed outcomes. The Methodology documents the transformations and inclusion decisions applied to them.

title: Technical Analysis
text:
The Tourism Indicators
Two measures are used to characterize pre-pandemic tourism exposure. They are related, but they do not measure the same thing.
The primary indicator is international visitor spending as a percentage of GDP, compiled by Our World in Data (OWID). It compares gross spending by international visitors with the size of the destination economy. A higher value indicates that visitor spending is large relative to domestic economic output.
The complementary indicator is international tourism receipts as a percentage of total exports, from the World Bank’s World Development Indicators (WDI). It compares tourism receipts with the value of all other exports of goods and services. This provides a different view of tourism’s importance, particularly in economies with relatively small or concentrated export sectors.
Neither measure is a direct estimate of tourism’s contribution to GDP or of the share of domestic value added generated by tourism. They are proxies for different dimensions of economic exposure. Their definitions, source construction, and limitations are documented in the Data Dictionary.

Coverage and comparability
The OWID visitor-spending series provides substantially broader coverage for the study’s purposes. It is available for all 29 economies in the primary shock sample and extends through 2024 in the retrieved data. The WDI receipts series has no observations after 2020, and 2019 data are missing for 14 of the 35 economies in the WDI shock sample.
As a result, some WDI baseline averages rely on only 2017 and 2018 observations. The difference in coverage is important when interpreting comparisons between the two indicators.

How closely do the indicators correspond?
Across the 24 economies with both measures, the indicators are positively correlated. The Pearson correlation is approximately 0.77; the Spearman rank correlation is 0.86.
The broad rankings are therefore similar, but the indicators are not interchangeable. The export-based denominator can make tourism receipts appear especially important in economies with relatively limited non-tourism exports. The GDP-based denominator instead compares gross visitor spending with the overall scale of the economy.








Figure 1: OWID visitor spending (% GDP) and WDI tourism receipts (% exports), 2015–2019 averages. The two indicators are positively correlated across the common sample, but differences in their denominators produce meaningful differences in measured exposure.







The distribution of visitor spending
The primary OWID measure also reveals substantial variation within the 29-economy shock sample. In some destinations, international visitor spending is equivalent to a very large share of GDP; in others, it is comparatively modest.








Figure 2: International visitor spending as a percentage of GDP, 2015–2019 average. Each bar represents one economy in the primary OWID shock sample (N = 29). The open circle identifies Kiribati, whose baseline average is based on one annual observation.

title: Technical Analysis
text:
Tourism Exposure and the 2020 Shock
The principal analysis estimates the cross-sectional relationship between pre-pandemic tourism exposure and real GDP growth in 2020. GDP growth is measured using the World Bank WDI indicator NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG.
Eight specifications are estimated. They combine:

Two tourism indicators: OWID visitor spending and WDI tourism receipts.
Each indicator’s own shock sample and the 24-economy common sample.
Two baseline windows: 2015–2019 and 2017–2019.

This produces four specifications for each indicator and eight in total. The common-sample models are particularly useful: because they hold the country set constant, differences between the two indicators cannot be attributed simply to different sample composition.
All eight estimated slopes are negative. The strength of the relationship, however, varies substantially by indicator and sample. The table reports every principal specification, including confidence intervals and both unadjusted and Holm-adjusted p-values. The Holm correction is applied across the family of eight tests.

Primary measure: OWID visitor spending
The OWID visitor-spending measure produces the clearest and most consistent relationship with the 2020 economic shock.
In the primary 2015–2019 specification (M1), each additional percentage point of visitor spending relative to GDP is associated with approximately 0.31 percentage points lower real GDP growth in 2020. The model’s R² is 0.414, meaning the bivariate relationship accounts for about 41% of the cross-country variation in 2020 growth rates in this sample.
The result is similar using the shorter 2017–2019 baseline. The estimated slope is -0.320 and R² is 0.428. It is also slightly stronger in the 24-economy common sample: R² is 0.489 for the longer baseline and 0.493 for the shorter one.
All four OWID specifications remain statistically significant after the Holm adjustment. The consistency across baseline windows and sample definitions supports the conclusion that higher pre-pandemic visitor spending relative to GDP was strongly associated with a more severe 2020 contraction in this group of economies.








Figure 3: Pre-pandemic visitor spending and 2020 real GDP growth. OWID visitor spending as a percentage of GDP, averaged over 2015–2019, is plotted against 2020 real GDP growth for the 29-economy primary sample. The line represents the estimated bivariate OLS relationship. The open circle identifies Kiribati, whose baseline is based on one observation. The relationship is exploratory and does not establish causation. Sources: OWID / UN Tourism and WDI GDP growth.







Complementary measure: WDI tourism receipts
The WDI measure produces a weaker and less consistent relationship.
In the full WDI sample, the estimated relationship is negative but does not reach conventional statistical significance: R² is 0.100 for the 2015–2019 baseline and 0.097 for 2017–2019. The corresponding raw p-values are 0.064 and 0.069; neither remains significant after Holm adjustment.
The common-sample results are stronger. With the country set held constant at 24 economies, the WDI models produce R² values of 0.233 and 0.248. Their raw p-values are 0.017 and 0.013, respectively. However, both Holm-adjusted p-values are 0.053, just above the conventional 0.05 threshold.
The comparison is informative. The WDI measure points in the same general direction as the OWID measure, but the relationship is weaker and the statistical evidence less consistent. This difference remains when the analysis is restricted to the same 24 economies.








Figure 4: Four model specifications using the 2015–2019 baseline. The top row shows each indicator in its own sample; the bottom row shows both indicators in the common 24-economy sample. OWID visitor spending is shown on the left and WDI tourism receipts on the right. The open circles identify thin baselines. The comparison shows that the stronger OWID relationship is not simply a consequence of its different sample composition.













Figure 5: Common-sample comparison (N = 24). OWID visitor spending and WDI tourism receipts plotted against 2020 GDP growth for the same economies and baseline period. This focused comparison makes the difference in estimated relationships easier to see.

Sensitivity and Influential Observations
A cross-sectional analysis with relatively small samples can be sensitive to individual economies. The diagnostics therefore examine influential observations and test whether the main results depend on unusually thin baseline coverage.

Influential observations

The table reports the most influential economy in each model and compares the original estimate with the estimate after excluding that observation. The Maldives is the most influential observation in all four OWID models and in the two WDI common-sample models. Excluding it reduces the strength of the OWID relationship, but the estimated slopes remain negative and statistically significant in all four specifications. In the primary model, R² falls from 0.414 to 0.309, while the slope changes from -0.308 to -0.251.
The Maldives therefore makes the relationship more pronounced, but it does not create it.
Timor-Leste is the most influential observation in the two full-sample WDI models. Its combination of relatively high tourism receipts as a share of exports and a comparatively modest 2020 contraction runs against the overall negative relationship. Excluding it strengthens both full-sample WDI estimates.
The common-sample WDI models tell a less reassuring story. Excluding the Maldives weakens the estimates: M4’s raw p-value rises to 0.062, while M8’s is 0.048. These exclusion-model p-values have not been adjusted for multiple testing. The common-sample WDI relationship is therefore more sensitive to influential observations than the OWID relationship.
Taken together, the diagnostics support a fairly specific conclusion: the OWID relationship is not dependent on the Maldives, while the WDI results are more sensitive to which economies are included. It would be too broad to describe both indicators as equally robust to influential observations.


Coverage-restricted sensitivity
The principal models retain economies with thin baseline coverage, including Kiribati, which has one annual observation in the OWID baseline. A second sensitivity analysis restricts each model to economies with at least three annual observations in the relevant baseline window.
This is a check on the influence of limited coverage, not a guarantee that three observations provide a fully representative baseline.

The OWID results are highly stable. Across all four specifications, slope estimates change by no more than 0.006, R² declines only slightly, and the negative relationship remains statistically detectable (p < 0.001 throughout). The findings are therefore not driven by economies with sparse baseline coverage.
The WDI results are less consistent. The 2015–2019 estimates change little after excluding Kiribati. In the shorter 2017–2019 window, however, the restriction removes 14 of 35 economies. R² increases from 0.097 to 0.180, and the slope becomes somewhat more negative, but Spearman’s correlation changes little and the raw p-value remains just above 0.05 (0.055).
That change should be interpreted cautiously: the smaller WDI sample has a different composition, reflecting substantial gaps in baseline coverage. Overall, the sensitivity analysis reinforces the consistency of the OWID results, while the WDI measure remains less conclusive and more vulnerable to coverage limitations.

title: Technical Analysis
text:
Economic Recovery Through 2024
The shock analysis identifies a strong relationship between pre-pandemic visitor spending and the severity of the 2020 contraction. The next question is whether that initial exposure was also associated with the subsequent recovery.
Recovery is examined using real GDP and real GDP per capita, each indexed to 2019 = 100. The two measures are calculated separately. Aggregate GDP tracks the total size of an economy; GDP per capita adjusts that output for population and therefore provides a different perspective on economic recovery.
The primary comparison year is 2024, the most recent year with near-complete coverage for the recovery sample. Twenty-eight of the 29 economies have real GDP data for that year. Data for 2025 are available for 22 economies and are preliminary estimates, so 2025 is treated as an additional, provisional observation rather than the principal recovery endpoint.

Coverage

Aggregate GDP trajectories
By 2024, 21 of the 28 economies with available data had returned to or exceeded their 2019 level of aggregate real GDP. The trajectories show a broad pattern of sharp contraction in 2020 followed by recovery over the subsequent years, although the depth of the initial decline and the pace of rebound varied considerably.








Figure 6: Real GDP recovery trajectories, 2015–2025 (2019 = 100). Lines are grouped by SIDS region. The horizontal reference at 100 marks each economy’s 2019 level. Annual sample sizes are shown below the chart. The 2025 observations are preliminary and cover a smaller set of economies.







Aggregate and per-capita recovery
Returning to the 2019 level of aggregate GDP does not necessarily mean that output per person has also recovered. Of the 28 economies with 2024 data, 20 had regained their 2019 real GDP per capita, compared with 21 that had regained aggregate real GDP. See Table 9 in the appendix for details.
The difference runs in both directions.
Four economies — Antigua and Barbuda, Papua New Guinea, Seychelles, and Vanuatu — had recovered aggregate GDP but remained below their 2019 level of GDP per capita. This pattern is consistent with population growth outpacing the recovery in total output: the economy had regained its former size, but output per person had not.
Three economies — Curaçao, the Marshall Islands, and Tuvalu — had recovered GDP per capita but not aggregate GDP. This can occur when per-person output rises even as total output remains below its previous level, including in circumstances involving population decline or emigration. Population change is one possible explanation; this analysis does not isolate its contribution.
Seven economies remained below their 2019 level of aggregate real GDP in 2024: Cuba, Curaçao, the Marshall Islands, the Solomon Islands, Suriname, Trinidad and Tobago, and Tuvalu.
The distinction matters. Aggregate GDP can return to its pre-pandemic level while output per person remains lower. Conversely, per-capita output can recover even while the total economy remains smaller. Neither measure captures the full experience of households, workers, or businesses, but together they provide a more complete picture than aggregate output alone.


Recovery and pre-pandemic tourism exposure
The relationship between pre-pandemic visitor spending and the 2024 aggregate GDP index is much less evident than the relationship between visitor spending and the initial 2020 contraction.
Across the 28 economies with 2024 data, the Pearson correlation between pre-pandemic OWID visitor spending and the 2024 aggregate GDP index is 0.21 (p = 0.275). This is not statistically significant. The result does not establish that the two variables are unrelated; it indicates that this analysis does not detect a clear linear association in this sample.








Figure 7: Pre-pandemic visitor spending and 2024 real GDP index (2019 = 100). Each point represents one economy in the recovery sample with available 2024 data (N = 28). The estimated Pearson correlation is 0.21 (p = 0.275).





The contrast with the shock analysis is notable. Pre-pandemic visitor spending was strongly associated with the severity of the initial contraction, but it offers little indication of where an economy stood relative to its 2019 aggregate GDP level four years later.
That does not mean the initial shock was harmless, or that tourism-dependent economies proved resilient. A single comparison year cannot capture the full path between 2020 and 2024. It does not show how long economies remained below their previous output levels, how much employment was lost, what debt accumulated during the disruption, or which businesses failed to reopen.
The recovery analysis is also limited to aggregate real GDP and real GDP per capita. It does not directly measure household income, employment quality, inequality, public finances, or the distribution of recovery gains. Those dimensions may tell a different story.

title: Technical Analysis
text:
Findings and Limits
Three findings emerge from the analysis.
First, the initial economic shock was strongly associated with pre-pandemic visitor spending relative to GDP. Across the four OWID specifications, the estimated relationship is negative, substantial, and remains statistically significant after adjustment for multiple testing. The result holds across both baseline windows and both sample definitions.
Second, the choice of tourism indicator matters. WDI tourism receipts as a share of exports point in the same general direction, but the relationship is weaker and less consistent. The difference persists in the common sample, where both indicators are tested against the same 24 economies. The measures capture related but distinct dimensions of exposure.
Third, the initial shock does not explain the 2024 recovery position. Most economies in the recovery sample had regained their 2019 aggregate GDP by 2024, but seven had not. The relationship between pre-pandemic visitor spending and the 2024 aggregate GDP index is not statistically significant. Aggregate and per-capita recovery also differ for several economies, underscoring that a return to the previous size of an economy is not necessarily a return to its previous level of output per person.
These findings should be interpreted within the limits of the design. The shock models are exploratory, bivariate, cross-sectional regressions. They describe associations across a diverse group of economies; they do not establish that tourism exposure caused a particular contraction. Other factors — including economic structure, fiscal capacity, public-health restrictions, policy responses, and pre-existing economic conditions — are not controlled for in these models.
The primary baseline window was selected after the shorter-window results had been examined. Both windows are reported, and the choice is documented in the Methodology, but the primary specification was not preregistered. The sample sizes are modest, the tourism indicators have uneven coverage, and some baseline averages rely on fewer annual observations than others.
The recovery comparison is narrower still. It uses one endpoint, 2024, and two measures of national output. It cannot identify the mechanisms behind different recovery trajectories or establish whether households and workers experienced the same recovery as national accounts.
The evidence is therefore strongest on the initial shock: economies where gross international visitor spending was large relative to GDP tended to experience deeper contractions when international travel collapsed. The evidence is considerably less informative about the longer-term recovery. That distinction is central to interpreting the results.

title: Island Time, Interrupted
text:
In 2020, international travel ground to a halt. Borders closed, flights disappeared, hotels emptied, and global tourist arrivals fell by roughly 74 percent1.
For some small island economies, this was more than a crisis for the hospitality industry. International visitors were an enormous source of economic activity. When they stopped coming, a substantial stream of spending disappeared with them.
Were the islands most exposed to international tourism also the hardest hit? And did they take longer to recover?
The first answer is a fairly emphatic yes. The second is more complicated.

title: Island Time, Interrupted
text:
In 2020, international travel ground to a halt. Borders closed, flights disappeared, hotels emptied, and global tourist arrivals fell by roughly 74 percent1.
For some small island economies, this was more than a crisis for the hospitality industry. International visitors were an enormous source of economic activity. When they stopped coming, a substantial stream of spending disappeared with them.
Were the islands most exposed to international tourism also the hardest hit? And did they take longer to recover?
The first answer is a fairly emphatic yes. The second is more complicated.

title: Island Time, Interrupted
text:
The 2020 Shock
Tourism exposure varies enormously across small island economies. Before the pandemic, international visitor spending in Aruba and the Maldives was equivalent to roughly 60 percent of GDP. In other economies, it represented a much smaller share.








Figure 1: International visitor spending as a share of GDP, 2015–2019 average. Sources: Our World in Data / UN Tourism





That difference mattered when travel collapsed.








Figure 2: Pre-pandemic visitor spending (2015–2019 average) versus 2020 real GDP growth. Sources: Our World in Data / UN Tourism; WDI NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG (constant 2015 USD).





Across 29 economies in the Caribbean, Pacific, and AIMS regions, higher pre-pandemic visitor spending was strongly associated with a deeper economic contraction in 2020. Each additional percentage point of visitor spending relative to GDP corresponded to approximately 0.31 percentage points lower GDP growth. The relationship accounted for about 41 percent of the variation across the sample.
The Maldives, with visitor spending equivalent to roughly 59 percent of GDP, experienced the sample’s steepest contraction. It also has considerable statistical influence. But excluding it weakens rather than eliminates the relationship.
A second tourism indicator, measuring receipts as a share of exports, produces a weaker and less consistent result. The choice of measure matters: the relationship is clearest when tourism exposure is compared with the overall size of the economy.
These are associations, not proof of causation. But the pattern is striking.

title: Island Time, Interrupted
text:
Recovery: Messier Than the Shock
By 2024, 21 of the 28 economies with available data had regained or exceeded their 2019 level of aggregate real GDP.








Figure 3: Real GDP trajectories, 2015–2025. Index: 2019 = 100. Source: WDI NY.GDP.MKTP.KD (constant 2015 USD). 2025 figures are preliminary.





Yet aggregate GDP tells only part of the story. Just 20 of those 28 economies had also regained their 2019 level of real GDP per capita. Four had recovered total output without recovering output per person; three showed the reverse.
Seven economies remained below their 2019 aggregate GDP level. Several were already facing significant economic difficulties before COVID-19.
And here’s the twist: pre-pandemic tourism exposure was not significantly associated with where economies stood relative to their 2019 aggregate GDP in 2024.
The islands most exposed to the initial shock did not necessarily end up furthest behind. Nor does a return to previous GDP tell us how many jobs disappeared, how much debt accumulated, or which businesses never reopened.

Getting Back Isn’t the Same as Recovering
The pandemic exposed a clear vulnerability: economies where international visitor spending was large relative to GDP generally suffered deeper contractions when travel stopped.
But the subsequent recovery followed no equally clear pattern. Initial exposure tells us a good deal about the shock, and considerably less about what came afterward.
GDP measures the size of an economy. It doesn’t tell the whole story of how people experienced its disruption or recovery.
Getting an economy back to its previous size is not quite the same as putting it back together.

title: Methodology
text:
This page documents how Island Time, Interrupted was designed and conducted: how the candidate universe and analytical samples were defined, how indicators were constructed, why particular specifications were chosen, and how limitations were handled.
The Data Dictionary documents the sources, variables, definitions, and coverage. The Technical Analysis presents the results. This page explains the decisions and procedures behind them.

title: Methodology
text:
Research Design

Research questions
The analysis addresses two related questions:

Was greater pre-pandemic exposure to international visitor spending associated with more severe economic contractions in 2020?
Was pre-pandemic tourism exposure associated with the extent of economic recovery by 2024?

The unit of analysis is the economy. The study covers candidate small island developing states (SIDS) across the Caribbean, Pacific, and Atlantic, Indian Ocean, and South China Sea (AIMS) regions.


Analytical approach
This is an exploratory, cross-sectional analysis. The shock analysis uses bivariate ordinary least squares (OLS) regression to examine the relationship between a pre-pandemic tourism indicator and annual real GDP growth in 2020. Pearson and Spearman correlations provide complementary measures of linear association and rank correspondence.
The recovery analysis uses indexed real GDP and real GDP per capita to compare each economy’s output with its 2019 level.
The models are deliberately bivariate. They do not control for fiscal capacity, economic structure, pre-existing economic conditions, pandemic restrictions, policy responses, or other factors that may have influenced the economic shock and recovery.
The purpose is to describe the cross-country patterns, not to isolate the independent effect of tourism. The analysis identifies associations; it does not establish causation.

title: Methodology
text:
Candidate Universe and Classification

Building the universe
The candidate universe was constructed from the UN Office of the High Representative for the Least Developed Countries, Landlocked Developing Countries and Small Island Developing States (UN-OHRLLS) list of SIDS, retrieved November 2026.
It contains 58 economies:



Classification
Economies




OHRLLS-listed SIDS
39


Associate Member SIDS
18


Other island economy
1


Total
58



The classification preserves several distinctions:

OHRLLS-listed SIDS: Includes the Cook Islands and Niue, which appear on the SIDS list despite not being UN General Assembly members.
Associate Member SIDS: Includes associate members of UN Regional Commissions, most of which are non-sovereign territories.
Other island economy: Bonaire, Sint Eustatius, and Saba (BES) are included for regional completeness, but are not classified as a SIDS group member.

Bahrain was excluded because it does not appear on the current OHRLLS list.


From candidates to observations
The candidate universe is not the same as the analytical panel. Economies enter the panel when at least one source provides observations. The resulting panel contains 57 economies; BES has no rows in the retrieved sources.
The shock-analysis samples are then determined by tourism-indicator availability and 2020 GDP growth. These are data-driven inclusion rules, not judgments about which economies are substantively representative.

title: Methodology
text:
Sample Construction

Fixed membership
Sample membership is defined using the availability of the relevant tourism indicator during 2017–2019 and 2020 GDP growth.
The 2017–2019 period is used to establish membership because it is the most recent three-year pre-pandemic window. Once defined, membership remains fixed when the alternative 2015–2019 baseline is calculated. This prevents changes in sample composition from being mistaken for differences between baseline specifications.


Sample hierarchy

The two indicator-specific shock samples overlap but are not identical. The common sample provides a way to compare the indicators while holding the economies constant.
Economies outside the shock samples are excluded because of missing tourism baselines, missing 2020 GDP growth, or both. The exclusions are documented in data/processed/country_coverage.csv.
The recovery sample follows the primary OWID shock sample. All 29 economies have a 2019 real GDP observation, although coverage declines in later years.

title: Methodology
text:
Constructing Tourism Baselines

Indicators
Two indicators are used to represent different dimensions of international tourism exposure:

International visitor spending as a percentage of GDP, from Our World in Data (OWID).
International tourism receipts as a percentage of total exports, from the World Bank’s World Development Indicators (WDI).

These measures have different denominators and are not interchangeable. Neither is a direct measure of tourism’s contribution to domestic value added. They are treated as exposure proxies, not as estimates of tourism’s share of GDP.


Baseline windows
Two pre-pandemic windows are calculated:



Specification
Years
Purpose




Primary
2015–2019
Broader measure of pre-pandemic exposure


Sensitivity
2017–2019
More recent pre-pandemic conditions



The longer window provides a broader average that is less dependent on any single year. The shorter window focuses on conditions immediately preceding the pandemic.
An important qualification: The 2015–2019 primary window was evaluated after the 2017–2019 results had been examined. The primary specification was not preregistered or selected before inspecting the data. Both windows are reported in full rather than presenting only the more favorable result.


Calculation
For each economy and indicator, the baseline is the arithmetic mean of the available annual observations within the selected window:
\[
\bar{x}_{i} = \frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{t \in T_i} x_{it}
\]
where \(x_{it}\) is the annual indicator value for economy \(i\), and \(T_i\) is the set of available years within the baseline window.
No missing annual values are filled. An economy with four available years in a five-year window receives a four-year mean, not an imputed five-year average. The number of observations contributing to each baseline is retained for coverage assessment.


Thin baselines
A baseline based on only one annual observation is flagged as thin. Kiribati is the only economy with a one-observation baseline in the primary OWID shock sample, and it is also thin in the shorter OWID window.
Thin baselines are retained in the principal models rather than excluded by default. Their influence is examined separately through a coverage-restricted sensitivity analysis.

title: Methodology
text:
Modeling the 2020 Shock

Outcome and explanatory variables
The outcome is annual real GDP growth in 2020, measured using WDI indicator NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG.
The explanatory variable is the pre-pandemic tourism baseline, measured separately using each of the two indicators.
The estimated model is:
\[
GDPGrowth_{i,2020} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 TourismExposure_i + \epsilon_i
\]
The slope \(\beta_1\) describes the average change in 2020 GDP growth associated with a one-percentage-point increase in the tourism exposure indicator.
For the OWID measure, this means a one-percentage-point increase in visitor spending relative to GDP. For the WDI measure, it means a one-percentage-point increase in tourism receipts relative to total exports.
The slope is an association across economies, not a causal effect.


Eight principal specifications
The models vary along three dimensions:



Dimension
Specifications




Tourism indicator
OWID visitor spending; WDI tourism receipts


Sample
Indicator-specific sample; common sample


Baseline window
2015–2019; 2017–2019



This produces eight principal models: four for each indicator, using its own sample and the common 24-economy sample across both baseline windows.
The common-sample specifications are particularly useful because they hold country membership constant when comparing the two indicators. Differences in results are therefore less likely to be explained simply by different sample composition.


Statistical reporting
Each model reports:

Sample size
Estimated slope
95% confidence interval
R-squared
Pearson correlation
Spearman rank correlation
Raw p-value
Holm-adjusted p-value

Holm’s step-down procedure is applied across the family of eight principal model p-values. This provides a multiple-testing adjustment while retaining the complete set of specifications. Because the models share economies and related explanatory variables, their tests are not independent; the adjustment should be interpreted in that context.

title: Methodology
text:
Sensitivity and Influence Diagnostics
Small cross-sectional samples can be sensitive to individual observations. Two checks are used to examine that risk.

Influential observations
Cook’s distance is calculated for each principal regression. The conventional reference threshold of \(4/N\) is used to flag potentially influential observations.
The most influential economy is then excluded in a diagnostic rerun of the relevant model. These exclusions are reported separately and do not replace the principal estimates.
This distinction matters. An influential observation is not necessarily erroneous. The Maldives, for example, represents a genuine case of exceptionally high tourism exposure. Removing it from the primary analysis would remove an economically meaningful part of the phenomenon being studied.
The exclusion checks therefore ask whether the estimated relationship depends disproportionately on a particular economy, not whether that economy should be removed from the study.


Coverage-restricted models
A second sensitivity analysis restricts each model to economies with at least three annual observations in the relevant baseline window.
This tests whether thin baselines materially affect the results. It also reveals the cost of uneven source coverage.
The most consequential case is the WDI 2017–2019 full-sample specification. Requiring three annual observations reduces the sample from 35 to 21 economies. Fourteen economies are excluded because their available WDI receipts observations are insufficient for the restriction.
The restricted model remains negative, but its statistical evidence is weaker. This result must be interpreted alongside the substantial reduction in sample size and the uneven availability of the underlying indicator.
The coverage restriction is a diagnostic choice, not a claim that three observations guarantee a representative baseline.

title: Methodology
text:
Constructing the Recovery Index

Index calculation
Recovery is measured using two WDI series:

Aggregate real GDP: NY.GDP.MKTP.KD
Real GDP per capita: NY.GDP.PCAP.KD

Each series is indexed independently to its 2019 value:
\[
Index_{i,t} = \left(\frac{Value_{i,t}}{Value_{i,2019}}\right)\times 100
\]
An index of 100 indicates a return to the 2019 level. Values above 100 indicate output greater than the 2019 level; values below 100 indicate output that remains lower.
Because the index is calculated relative to each economy’s own 2019 value, the comparison concerns recovery to a pre-pandemic level, not the absolute size of economies relative to one another.


Why 2019?
2019 is used as the reference year because it is the last full calendar year before the pandemic disrupted international travel. Earlier observations from 2015–2018 are retained to show the pre-pandemic trajectory.


Why 2024?
The primary recovery comparison uses 2024, the most recent year with near-complete coverage across the recovery sample. Twenty-eight of the 29 economies have an available observation; the U.S. Virgin Islands does not.
Data for 2025 are available for 22 economies, but those observations are preliminary and cover a smaller subset. They are retained where available and flagged as preliminary, but are not used for the principal cross-economy recovery comparison.


Aggregate and per-capita measures
Aggregate GDP and GDP per capita are calculated separately because they answer different questions.
Aggregate GDP measures the total output of an economy. GDP per capita adjusts for population and provides a measure of output relative to the number of residents.
The two can move in different directions. An economy can regain its previous total output while remaining below its previous output per person, or recover output per person while its total economy remains smaller.
Population growth, decline, and migration may help explain these differences, but the index alone cannot identify the mechanisms. The analysis therefore reports both measures without attributing their divergence to a specific cause.

title: Methodology
text:
Missing Data and Assumptions
The analysis uses available observations without filling gaps through statistical imputation.







Situation
Treatment




Missing annual tourism observations
Baseline calculated from available years


No tourism observations in a baseline window
No baseline; excluded from that indicator’s shock sample


Missing 2020 GDP growth
Excluded from shock models


Missing 2019 real GDP
No recovery index can be calculated


Missing later-year GDP
Economy omitted from that year’s recovery comparison


Source-published preliminary estimates
Retained as supplied and flagged where applicable



No missing observations are imputed by this analysis. Source-published estimates are retained as supplied; their preliminary status is made explicit where relevant.
Several assumptions and limitations follow from these choices:

The two tourism indicators are treated as proxies for economic exposure, not direct measures of tourism value added.
Annual GDP growth captures the calendar-year contraction, not the timing or duration of restrictions within each economy.
The cross-sectional models do not account for differences in economic structure, policy response, fiscal capacity, or pre-existing economic conditions.
The baseline averages vary in the number of annual observations contributing to them.
The recovery index measures national output relative to 2019, not household welfare, employment quality, inequality, or the distribution of recovery gains.

These constraints define what the analysis can reasonably claim. They are not problems that can be resolved simply by adding more decimal places to the estimates.

title: Methodology
text:
Reproducibility

Software and packages
The analysis was conducted in R 4.4.1 and rendered using Quarto.
Principal packages include:
tidyr, dplyr, wbstats, scales, here, knitr, and ggplot2.


Script execution
The project separates acquisition, quality assessment, exploratory analysis, shock modeling, and recovery analysis into sequential scripts:
source("R/01_data_acquisition.R")
source("R/02_data_quality.R")
source("R/03_preliminary_eda.R")
source("R/04_shock_models.R")
source("R/05_recovery_analysis.R")
The acquisition script retrieves WDI observations through wbstats::wb_data(). Subsequent scripts construct the analytical panel, evaluate coverage, calculate baselines, estimate the models, run sensitivity checks, and construct recovery indices.


Rendering
The Quarto project is rendered with:
quarto render
The resulting site is published from the docs/ directory through GitHub Pages.


Data retrieval and updates
The WDI retrieval date and returned indicator codes are recorded in:
data/raw/worldbank/wdi_retrieval_metadata.txt
OWID CSV files in data/raw/ are fixed downloads from 2026 and do not update automatically. Updated OWID data require a fresh download and replacement of the local files.
WDI data are retrieved through the World Bank API and may change between runs as source data are revised.
Processed datasets, source metadata, and the project scripts are retained in the repository to support inspection and reproduction of the analysis.
